The Apple Health app on iPhone is a powerful health data tracking tool. Whether it's logging data from your Apple Watch, importing records directly from your doctor, or integrating with third-party apps, there's a feature for everyone.

Here are ways to make the most of the Apple Health app.

Apple Watch

This one is obvious. As you'd expect, the Apple Watch and Apple Health are a perfect match. While you can see a lot of your Apple Watch data in the Apple Fitness app, the Apple Health app gives you a more comprehensive overview of your health.

The Apple Health app logs data from your Apple Watch, such as steps, heart rate, resting heart rate, and more. While the Apple Fitness app focuses mainly on workout data, the Apple Health app provides an outstanding overall health perspective, including historical data and trend analysis.

  • 40mm Apple Watch SE 3: $219 starting (original price $249)
  • 44mm Apple Watch SE 3: $249 starting (original price $279)
  • 42mm Apple Watch Series 11: $299 starting (original price $399)
  • 46mm Apple Watch Series 11: $329 starting (original price $429)
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3: $779 starting (original price $799)

If you're not interested in the Apple Watch, third-party fitness trackers can also integrate with Apple Health. WHOOP is a good fitness band platform that can connect with Apple Health. Smart rings are also becoming increasingly popular, including the Oura Ring and Ultrahuman Ring.

Track More Data

Beyond data collected by wearables like the Apple Watch, there are other accessories that can log important vital signs to the Apple Health app.

One of my most-used accessories is the Withings BPM Connect. I try to take my blood pressure every day, and the Withings BPM Connect makes it really easy. After I take my blood pressure, the results are automatically sent to the Apple Health app. I can monitor trends there and analyze the data alongside other metrics from the day.

The OMRON Evolv is another popular blood pressure monitor that supports Apple Health integration, and it's now even cheaper than the Withings BPM Connect.

The Apple Health app also supports integration with smart scales. I step on my scale every morning when I wake up, and the data is automatically saved to the Apple Health app with no extra action needed. Options in this category basically cover every price point. I've been using a fairly basic Withings Body Smart Scale for years now. Withings has options at various price points, including the top-tier Withings Body Scan, which tracks more data.

I mostly stick to the Withings ecosystem when I can, but other companies also make smart scales. The Wyze Scale Ultra is a popular option under $50, and the Wyze Smart Scale X Butterfly is also under $33.

While blood pressure and weight are the main metrics I track with third-party accessories, the Apple Health app also supports integration with smart thermometers, smart sleep tracking devices, glucose monitors, and more.

Here, you can add your medical records account and sync the data to the Health app. Availability will vary depending on your doctor. Generally speaking, most doctors and hospitals that integrate with MyChart should show up as an option.

  • Open Health
  • Tap your profile picture in the top right corner
  • Tap 'Medical Records'

Connect your medical records

The Apple Health app can also integrate directly with your doctor's medical records. This includes lab results, allergies, vaccinations, medical history, surgical records, and more.

Reorganize Apple Health Layout

So, after you put all this data into the Apple Health app, reorganizing the layout is important so you can see your most important metrics first. After that, you can dig in manually when you have time.

To do this, simply open the Health app and find the 'Edit' button in the top right. From here, you can drag and drop different data metrics, pin them, and arrange them in the order you like. For example, I like to put steps at the top, followed by heart rate data, my Sleep Score, blood oxygen, weight, and blood pressure.

Once you've selected and organized all your pinned data metrics, you can scroll down and select 'Show All Health Data' for a deeper look.

Manage Data Sources

Within the Health app, one important thing is setting the priority of your data sources and making sure you know when multiple apps or devices are writing to the same metric.

Here's how to manage which apps have read and write access to your Health app:

  • Open the Health app
  • Select 'Apps,' where you'll find granular controls for specific data types and apps

For example, I restrict the Withings app to only write weight and blood pressure data. I don't want it doing too much and arbitrarily putting other data into my Health database.

You can also set the priority of different sources for specific metrics:

  • Open the Health app
  • Tap a metric
  • Scroll down and select 'Data Sources & Access'
  • Tap 'Edit' in the top right corner
  • From here, you can select your data sources. For some metrics, you can also set the priority of different sources by dragging.

Trends and Highlights

The Apple Health app will also proactively show you key trends and highlights. For example, one of my current trends is 'average daily steps have increased over the past 14 weeks.'

On the other hand, highlights are an overview focused on recent data and real-time tracking of your progress. For example, one of my current highlights shows 'fewer steps than usual taken today so far.'

Medical ID and Sharing

In the Health app, you'll see a 'Sharing' tab in the bottom navigation bar. From there, you can choose to share your health data with people close to you or your doctor. You can select specific metrics to share. You can revoke sharing at any time. All data is encrypted, and what's shared is a summary of each item, not the specific details.

You should also take a little time to set up your Medical ID in the Apple Health app. To do this, open the Health app, tap your profile picture, then select Medical ID.

You can choose to display your Medical ID when your iPhone is locked and share it during emergency calls. The Medical ID includes your age, allergies, medications, height, weight, and more.

The Apple Health app is one of my favorite apps on my iPhone. I love how it can pull together data from the Apple Watch, Oura Ring, and third-party apps and accessories like Withings. Instead of bouncing around between multiple third-party apps, everything can be found in Apple Health, and I can get a quick daily snapshot of where my health metrics stand.
